w: Poland's third-largest national park guards the wildest stretch of the Carpathians - grass-topped ridges called polonina, primeval beech forest, and enough remoteness that wolves, bears and lynx still roam freely. Its beech stands were folded into a UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2021.
_facts: third-largest national park in Poland, in the extreme southeast corner (Subcarpathian Voivodeship)
became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 as an extension of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests listing

w: A 640-metre mountain pass carrying a rail tunnel that has been demolished and rebuilt more than once. Russian and Austro-Hungarian troops bled for it through the winter of 1914-15, and the line itself - a vital link across the Carpathians since 1874 - only reopened to regular passenger service in 1999.
s: A pass fought over, its tunnel rebuilt three times.
_facts: mountain pass on the Poland-Slovakia border, 640 m elevation
642 m railway tunnel finished 1874, linking Galicia to the Austro-Hungarian Empire
bitterly contested in WWI Eastern Front battles in winter 1914-15
tunnel demolished and rebuilt multiple times across both world wars, regular passenger rail resumed only in 1999

w: A Hasidic synagogue that served Lesko's Jewish community until the Nazis emptied it in 1942. The building sat desecrated for decades before reopening in the 1980s as part of the Museum of the Jews of Galicia - its old walls now holding the history that once tried to erase them.
s: A desecrated synagogue turned Jewish museum.
_facts: former Hasidic synagogue in Lesko, functioned as a place of worship until 1942
deserted by the Nazis during WWII
in the 1980s repurposed as part of the Museum of the Jews of Galicia

w: A grass-topped montane ridge with four summits, the highest reaching 1,297 metres. Climb it on a clear day and the whole roll call of Bieszczady's big peaks lines up - Tarnica, Halicz, even Ukraine's Gorgany and, on rare days, the distant Tatras. One of the range's signature panoramas.
s: A grassy ridge with the region's best panorama.
_facts: montane ecosystem (polonina) in the Bieszczady Mountains between the Dwernik and Wolosaty valleys
four major culminations, highest is Kruhly Wierch at 1,297 m
view from the peak takes in Wielka Rawka, Polonina Wetlinska, Tarnica, Halicz, and on clear days Ukraine's Gorgany or the Tatra Mountains

w: The highest peak within Poland's borders at 1,346 metres, and one of the country's official Crown Peaks - a twin-summited massif whose steep rock face towers 500 metres straight over the Wolosatka valley. Easy to pick out from its neighbours by that distinctive double-topped silhouette.
s: The highest peak in Poland's Bieszczady.
_facts: highest peak in the Bieszczady Mountains within Poland at 1,346 m
one of the Polish Crown Peaks
summit towers 500 m above the Wolosatka Valley
has two summits, 1,339 m and 1,346 m

w: A 1,272-metre summit whose small mountaintop pasture opens onto one of Bieszczady's best views - Tarnica, Polonina Wetlinska and Carynska all lined up at once. Rare Carpathian flora clings to its slopes, a fifteen-minute ridge walk from its taller neighbour, Wielka Rawka.
s: A modest peak with an outsized panorama.
_facts: peak in the western Bieszczady Mountains near Ustrzyki Gorne, 1,272 m
excellent vantage point for the Tarnica group, Polonina Wetlinska and Carynska
15 minutes by trail from Wielka Rawka
rare plants recorded here including Carpathian tocia and rock bird cherry

w: A medieval castle ruin perched over the San river valley at the foot of the Eastern Carpathians, first recorded in the 14th century under the name Soban. Little survives above the footings now, but the site still commands the same river bend it was built centuries ago to watch over.
s: A medieval ruin watching the San river bend.
_facts: medieval castle in the San river valley, in Manasterzec village, Lesko County
recorded as Soban in 1372, castro Sobyen in 1460

w: A Swiss-style monastery of Nazarene nuns, built on a mountain meadow and consecrated in 1931 - the sisters hid wanted priests and Jewish people here through the Nazi occupation, even while German soldiers were billeted in the same building. Later, Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski was interned within its walls through 1955-56.
s: A convent that hid fugitives from the Nazis.
_facts: monastery of Sisters of the Holy Family of Nazareth in Komancza, opened May 1928, building consecrated 1931
German soldiers quartered in the monastery during Nazi occupation; nuns hid wanted priests and Jewish people
Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski was interned there from 29 October 1955 to 28 October 1956

w: A protected sweep of the upper San river valley, established in 1992 and threaded with the remnants of a landscape once far more populated than it is today - a vanished village at Krywe, an old mill at Smolnik, cemeteries at Stuposiany and Ruskie, and a lone wooden cerkiew at Hulskie.
s: A river valley haunted by vanished villages.
_facts: landscape park in Podkarpackie Voivodeship, established 1992, covering 342.70 sq km
contains three nature reserves plus designated complexes: village of Krywe, village of Smolnik, cerkiew and mill at Hulskie, cemeteries at Stuposiany and Ruskie

w: An 18th-century Jewish cemetery serving Ustrzyki Dolne and its surrounding villages, likely dating from before the town's rise. Partly destroyed during the Second World War, it was never restored to the official monuments register - a quiet, unmarked reminder of a community erased from this corner of the Carpathians.
s: An unlisted Jewish burial ground from the 1700s.
_facts: cemetery of the Jewish community of Ustrzyki Dolne, likely established 18th century
partially destroyed during WWII
not listed in the register of historical monuments

w: Established in the first half of the 18th century for Baligrod's Jewish community, devastated by the Germans in the Second World War and left to decay for decades afterward. It was only entered onto the register of historical monuments in 1990 - long after the community it served was gone.
s: A Jewish cemetery devastated, then forgotten.
_facts: cemetery of the Jewish community of Baligrod and surrounding villages, established first half of 18th century
devastated by the Germans during WWII, fell into disrepair afterward
entered into the register of monuments in 1990

w: An 18th-century Gothic wooden church standing alone in the small village of Smolnik, one of the scattered tserkvas that together earned UNESCO World Heritage status as the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region - a shingled Orthodox survivor amid Bieszczady's emptied Lemko villages.
_facts: Gothic wooden church in Smolnik, 18th century
part of the UNESCO Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region (Poland and Ukraine) listing

w: Poland's largest dam, a concrete gravity wall completed in 1968 that throttles the San river and, in doing so, created Lake Solina - the biggest artificial lake in the country, filling what had been a river valley in the heart of the Bieszczady mountains.
s: Poland's biggest dam, and its biggest artificial lake.
_facts: concrete gravity dam in Solina, Lesko County, Bieszczady
largest dam in Poland
completed 1968, created Lake Solina, the largest artificial lake in Poland

w: A 510-square-kilometre buffer zone shielding Bieszczady National Park's western flank, established in 1992 and folded around seven nature reserves, including two stands of ancient yew. Bears, wolves, lynx and wildcats still roam its multi-storey mountain forest, largely undisturbed by tourism.
s: A wild buffer zone thick with bears and wolves.
_facts: landscape park in Subcarpathian Voivodeship, established 1992, covering 510.14 sq km
buffer zone of Bieszczady National Park to the west, contains seven nature reserves including two yew reserves
home to bears, wolves, lynxes and wildcats
